title: Dry bones (Ezekiel 37:1–14)
hook: a valley of bones rattles together, and breath comes into them

segments.voice: Yesterday, a field at Anathoth bought in wartime, and your line: houses will be bought again.

Jeremiah stayed in Jerusalem. Another prophet, Ezekiel, a priest, was among the exiles already taken to Babylon, living by a river there. His visions are strange and vast: wheels full of eyes, a scroll he's told to eat, a Temple measured out cubit by cubit. Then news reaches the exiles: Jerusalem has fallen. The Temple is gone. And the people say: our bones are dried up. Our hope is lost. We're cut off. Into that, Ezekiel is carried by the spirit and set down in a valley.
screen: `EZEKIEL AMONG THE EXILES.` → `JERUSALEM HAS FALLEN.` → `OUR HOPE IS LOST.` → `SET DOWN IN A VALLEY.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "The hand of the LORD was upon me, and carried me out in the spirit of the LORD, and set me down in the midst of the valley which was full of bones." He's led around them: very many, and very dry. Long dead. And God asks: "Son of man, can these bones live?" Ezekiel's answer is careful, almost wise: "O Lord GOD, thou knowest." Not yes. Not no. Then God tells him to prophesy to the bones: "O ye dry bones, hear the word of the LORD." He does, and there's a noise, a rattling, and the bones come together, bone to his bone. Sinews, then flesh, then skin. But no breath. Bodies, lying there. So God tells him to prophesy a second time, to the breath: come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe on these slain. Breath comes into them, and they live, and stand up on their feet, an exceeding great army. The word that holds it together is the Hebrew ruach, all through this passage, meaning breath, and wind, and spirit, all at once. The spirit carries Ezekiel. The breath enters the bodies. The four winds supply it. One word, and English needs three. Then God explains: these bones are the whole house of Israel. They say our hope is lost. I will open your graves and bring you home. Jewish communities read this vision on the Sabbath during Passover, the festival of freedom. Christians also hear in it the hope of resurrection, and of the Spirit who gives life.
screen: `A VALLEY FULL OF DRY BONES.` · `O LORD GOD, THOU KNOWEST.` · `BODIES, BUT NO BREATH.` · `RUACH: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT.` · then, large: `CAN THESE BONES LIVE?`

segments.voice: Breathe in deeply and feel the air arrive; you didn't make it. Then bring to mind something that feels like dry bones, a project, a hope, a friendship, a faith gone quiet, and ask Ezekiel's question honestly, can this live, without forcing an answer. With each breath in, picture breath moving toward it, and with each breath out, release your need to control it; if you pray, you can say: thou knowest.
Dry bones. Ezekiel's valley of the long dead, joined bone to bone and filled with breath: a picture of a people's hope coming back to life.
Your line: can these bones live? One word, ruach, for breath, wind and spirit. That's day four hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Ezekiel 37 is read at the Easter Vigil and at Pentecost in many churches, and has long been sung and preached in African American churches as a vision of hope; in Jewish practice it is the prophetic reading on the Sabbath during Passover.

fork.setup: you're standing in a valley full of very dry bones. God asks: can these bones live? what do you say?
options: no, they've been dead too long.
fork.reveal: Ezekiel says neither yes nor no: "O Lord GOD, thou knowest." then God tells him to speak to the bones.

chat.says: In that dry bones vision, what finally brings the bodies to life?
options: Breath. The bones join and get flesh, but live only when breath comes from the four winds.
The rattling. As soon as the bones snap together, they jump up as a living army.
Ezekiel's own hands. He sets each bone in place and blows into each one himself.
chat.meaning: After the first prophecy the bodies lie there with no breath. Only when breath comes from the four winds do they live and stand.

Ezekiel.meaning: a priest and prophet among the exiles in Babylon

ruach.meaning: Hebrew for breath, wind and spirit, all at once

sinews.meaning: the cords that tie muscle to bone

notes: The KJV of 37:3 reads 'Son of man, can these bones live? And I answered, O Lord GOD, thou knowest.' The voice splits it into the question and the answer. Confirm.

News of Jerusalem's fall reaching the exiles: Ezekiel 33:21. The placement of chapter 37 after that news is the book's order; confirm phrasing.
